body.text: Inside the legally 'murky' world of social media eats offering dinner for $10, metres away

On an overcast day in Sydney, content creator David Coluzzi pulls up in his car in front of 14-year-old Raheel and his mother. Raheel is holding a box full of neatly packed assorted scrolls that he has baked, ready to make a sale.
Mr Coluzzi thanks Raheel, also known as Roly, and goes back into his car to film himself eating the treats for his "trying food off Facebook Marketplace" social media series.
"It has changed everything for him, which was really rewarding for me to see," Mr Coluzzi said, thinking back to the meet-up.
But Facebook Marketplace isn't normally the first place people would look to grab a bite to eat when hungry; nor is it known for its food purchasing features.
However, with just a quick search, it is easy to find a range of food options to buy, sometimes just metres from your location.
Some are as cheap as just $10.
There are no food quality standards, and no guarantees that the person had proper training in food safety and handling.
That's what sets off alarms for Lydia Buchtmann, CEO of the Food Safety Information Council.
"It can be extremely dangerous," Ms Buchtmann said.
"You're working in a kitchen where you haven't had the training, or your family is around. You might have the cat running over the benchtop preparing food.
"It leaves you very vulnerable because you can get ill."
At the time, Roly complied with legal requirements and was careful that his food was safe, but experts say many don't.
Under Australian laws, businesses selling food must follow strict protocols that comply with food safety standards.
And there are legal repercussions if it's not done by the book.
"If you've made that curry, if someone actually tracks you down and you have got ill from it, you can be prosecuted," Ms Buchtmann said.
There's a myriad of things that could go wrong during the cooking and handling process if the guidelines are not followed, she said.
Ms Buchtmann likens amateur cooking without proper training to "driving a car" without a licence.
"However good a cook you are, and however great and clean you think your kitchen is, the domestic kitchen is not good enough to prepare food for others," she said.
Mr Coluzzi knows the risks involved but said he does it because he loves to "understand food from a different perspective".
"I'm not too clear about the legality of it. It does spark a lot of conversation in the comments. I try not to get too involved in it because it's not really what I'm doing it for," he said.
Finding a "new culture to experience" and tasting authentic cuisines from home cooks from different backgrounds keeps him enthusiastic about the experience.
"It's cool to just be able to find something different," he said.
So far, he hasn't gotten sick.
Mr Coluzzi said that in his Italian culture, when someone has invited you into their home to cook for you, it's seen as a "sign of respect".

"For me, it's not a foreign thing to go and eat from somebody else … I'm not an advertising service for these people. I am just someone going to share my experience and understand the person behind the food," Mr Coluzzi said.
Illegal vs legal food sales
It is illegal to sell food through online platforms such as Facebook Marketplace without the proper licences and qualifications.
Those who are selling on these platforms need to let their local council know to follow proper procedure. But enforcement of the regulations is light and varies across the country.
Under Australian laws, anyone selling food commercially, even from a home kitchen, must comply with the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code.

Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) is the independent statutory authority responsible for the development and maintenance of the code, which sets out the legal requirements for food produced or imported for sale in Australia and New Zealand to ensure a safe food supply for consumers.
While they set the standards, they do not enforce them. That responsibility falls on state and territory food regulatory agencies.
If a seller has cooked food from an unapproved home kitchen without registration, it is considered illegal.
There are some exceptions, such as food options from registered businesses or restaurants that already operate within food safety requirements.
But it's a murky area, according to Ms Buchtmann.
Food trucks, for example, may comply with the standards, but it may not be lawful for them to sell food outside of their registered business.
There are some exemptions, like low-risk, shelf-stable items, such as jams, honey, or baked goods that do not need refrigeration.
Private, one-off peer-to-peer sales on platforms such as Facebook Marketplace are generally exempt from standard Australian Consumer Law consumer guarantees.
This makes it difficult for buyers who become ill from food they've bought to seek compensation from the vendor.
Mr Coluzzi says he always makes sure people are aware of the legalities involved before filming.
"There have been situations [after filming] where people have gone and looked into making sure they're doing it the right way to make sure they're following the right process," he said.
The lemonade stand
Many of us remember growing up selling lemonade in the front yard, or helping out at our school sausage sizzle.
Would these also need to follow the same rules? Technically, yes. But it depends on the local council where you live and insurance compliance.
Sausage sizzles still need to register with their local council, according to Ms Buchtmann.
"Your local council will give you a temporary licence to prepare food there; make sure that's all done safely. And they hand out information on how to do a community-type event," she said.
There are options available for those who want to prepare food without access to a kitchen that meets these standards.
In the case of charity events, or preparing low-risk foods that do not require refrigeration, spaces can be provided at farmers' markets, she said.
Training and information are also readily available through the local council websites.
"If they're really keen, they need to do proper training," Ms Buchtmann said.
There are ways to protect yourself if you do want to buy food on Marketplace. Asking if the seller is registered and complies with council requirements can help determine if it is worth the risk.
Mr Coluzzi said he does his research before buying the food.
"There are a lot of businesses that are actually restaurants trying to put it on there too," he said.
